title: Paediatric inguinal herniotomy
subtitle: High ligation of the patent processus vaginalis

sources.title: Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: inguinal hernias and hydroceles
Assessment and management of inguinal hernias in children (Clinical Report, Pediatrics 2023)

indications: Inguinal hernia in an infant or child, reducible, on an elective list without undue delay.
Incarcerated hernia after successful reduction, once the oedema has settled.
Irreducible or strangulated hernia, as an emergency.
contraindications: A communicating hydrocele in an infant may resolve and is usually observed first.
Unstable intercurrent illness; ex-premature infants need a plan for post-operative apnoea monitoring rather than a contraindication.
preparation: Examine and document both sides and the position of both testes.
Consent including recurrence, testicular atrophy or ascent, injury to the vas, wound infection and the plan for the contralateral side.
Plan day-case or overnight stay according to gestation, post-menstrual age and comorbidity.
positioning: Supine with legs slightly apart, on a warmed mattress.
equipment: Fine paediatric instruments, small self-retaining or hand-held retractors, fine absorbable sutures.
Magnifying loupes are helpful for small infants.
anatomy: The hernia sac is the patent processus vaginalis, lying anteromedial to the cord within the cremaster.
In infants the inguinal canal is short; the internal and external rings almost overlie one another.
The vas deferens and testicular vessels are tiny and lie posterior to the sac. The vas is easily crushed by forceps.
The ilioinguinal nerve runs on the cord beneath the external oblique aponeurosis.
criticalSafety: Never grasp the vas or the vessels with forceps. Handle them only with the sac or by gentle sweeping.
Ligate the sac at the internal ring, at the level of the extraperitoneal fat.
Return the testis to the scrotum at the end and confirm its position.
structuresAtRisk: Bladder in a direct or medial dissection
Ovary or fallopian tube within the sac in girls
commonErrors: Tearing a thin sac in an infant, then losing its proximal end in the internal ring.
Low ligation that leaves a residual sac and causes recurrence.
Leaving the testis high in the canal, causing iatrogenic ascent.
complications: Recurrence, more common after incarceration and in premature infants.
Injury to the vas deferens, which may affect future fertility without any immediate sign.
Wound infection, haematoma, post-anaesthetic apnoea in ex-premature infants.
postop: Feeding as soon as awake; simple analgesia.
Apnoea monitoring for ex-premature infants per local criteria.
Advise parents on scrotal swelling, which usually settles, and to return for a new lump or a high testis.

steps.emphasis: Mark the side with the child awake and the parent present. Bilateral hernias are common; confirm what was consented.
Gestation and post-menstrual age decide the apnoea monitoring plan.
Antibiotics are not routinely needed for a clean elective herniotomy; follow local policy.
Include the scrotum in the field so the testis can be checked and repositioned.
Coordinate with any caudal or ilioinguinal block already given.
Subcuticular absorbable suture or tissue adhesive in a nappy area.

step.hern.access.title: Skin crease incision and opening the canal
step.hern.access.why: In an infant the rings nearly overlie each other, so the sac can often be reached through the external ring without opening the aponeurosis, minimising dissection around the cord.
how: Make a short incision in the lowest inguinal skin crease over the internal ring.
Divide Scarpa fascia and identify the external oblique aponeurosis and external ring.
In older children, open the aponeurosis in the line of its fibres, protecting the ilioinguinal nerve.
pitfalls: Making the incision too low, over the external ring in an older child, which hinders high ligation.

step.hern.sac.title: Separating the sac from the vas and vessels
step.hern.sac.why: This is the step that decides fertility and testicular viability. The structures at risk are millimetres wide and are injured by forceps pressure, not only by cutting.
how: Lift the cremaster and identify the sac on the anteromedial aspect of the cord.
Gently sweep the vas and vessels off the posterior surface of the sac with fine non-toothed instruments.
Divide the sac between clips once fully separated, and continue proximally to the internal ring.
In girls, check the sac for an ovary or tube before ligation.
pitfalls: Tearing a thin infant sac and losing its proximal end.

step.hern.ligate.title: High ligation of the sac
step.hern.ligate.why: Recurrence after herniotomy is usually a residual sac. Ligation must be at the internal ring, where the extraperitoneal fat appears.
how: Twist the sac to reduce any contents and confirm it is empty.
Transfix and ligate the neck at the level of the internal ring with an absorbable suture.
Excise the redundant sac and allow the stump to retract.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel or bladder within the sac
pitfalls: Ligating too low, below the internal ring.
Including bowel or ovary in the ligature.

step.hern.testis.title: Returning the testis to the scrotum
step.hern.testis.why: Traction during dissection often draws the testis up into the canal. Left there, it becomes an iatrogenic undescended testis.
how: Gently pull the testis down into the scrotum at the end of the procedure.
Confirm by palpation that it lies in the scrotum before the drapes come off.
Record the final position in the operation note.
pitfalls: Forgetting to check after a difficult dissection.
